*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Your app didn’t crash because of a bug. It crashed because the Indian government decided to block your backend.

Starting February 24th, https://t.co/cpotyIe5BS became unreachable across major Indian ISPs. Supabase later confirmed this was due to a ministry order. No prior notice. No public explanation. No transition window.

Jio. Airtel. ACT Fibernet. All started DNS-poisoning Supabase domains, redirecting API calls to a sinkhole IP. Every app running on Supabase in India (auth, database, edge functions, real-time) went dark for millions of users. Reports suggest Firebase Hosting is facing similar disruptions.

Thousands of startups, student projects, hackathon builds, production SaaS apps. Blocked. No “here’s 90 days to migrate.” Nothing.

Supabase had to publicly tag Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on X just to get someone to talk to them: “Supabase is used by millions of developers worldwide, and millions of users in India are currently unable to access our platform. Could we talk to someone in your team about this?”

Silence from MeitY. Silence from the Minister. Silence from every ISP.

Supabase is not a social media platform. It’s a PostgreSQL database wrapper with auth, storage, and APIs. Its users are engineers building software. There is no obvious legal or content-based reason to block it.

And this isn’t the first time. Medium blocked on Jio/Airtel in Oct 2025. Linktree blocked without explanation. BSNL blocked Dailymotion and Telegram links in Aug 2025. ACT Fibernet blocked TheMovieDB. Ubuntu mirrors and Cloudflare R2 hit before that.

Critical internet infrastructure keeps getting caught in opaque, unaccountable blocking orders. No public reasoning. No appeals process. No distinction between a piracy site and a developer tool.

The workaround? Switch DNS to 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. Use a VPN. Proxy backend traffic through custom domains so you’re not exposed to ISP blocks.

But think about what we’re saying. We’re telling Indian developers: “Your government might randomly block your backend, so architect around that.” That’s not a healthy ecosystem. That’s building on a minefield.

We talk about Digital India. Startup India. A $5 trillion economy. We want to compete globally in SaaS and AI.

But we’re blocking the tools our developers need to build. Without notice. Without reason. Without a plan.

India’s builders deserve better than this.

वर्तमान सरकार ने महँगाई पर मज़बूती से नियन्त्रण किया है । 2026 में स्थिति अलग है। आज की स्थिति में SCSS deposit पर 8.2% ब्याज और महंगाई लगभग 5% है, जिससे जमाकर्ताओं को वास्तविक लाभ (+3.2%) मिल रहा है। लोन दरें भी 2013 के लगभग 10% से अधिक से घटकर लगभग 7.5% से भी कम हो गई हैं। इससे EMI लगभग 15% तक कम हुई और लोगों पर वित्तीय बोझ घटा है।
इसके अलावा, वरिष्ठ नागरिकों के लिए डिजिटल लाइफ सर्टिफिकेट, डोरस्टेप बैंकिंग जैसी सुविधाएँ शुरू हुई हैं। कुल मिलाकर, अब ब्याज दरें और महंगाई का संतुलन जमाकर्ताओं व उधारकर्ताओं दोनों के लिए अनुकूल है और उनकी नियमित वित्तीय जरूरतों को बेहतर ढंग से पूरा करने में मदद कर रहा है।

4. नोटबंदी एक आर्थिक निर्णय था, जो काले धन, जाली मुद्रा तथा अवैध सीमा-पार वित्तपोषण पर अंकुश लगाने के लिए अत्यंत महत्वपूर्ण था। इससे अधिक लेन-देन को औपचारिक वित्तीय प्रणाली के दायरे में लाने में मदद मिली तथा यूपीआई जैसे डिजिटल भुगतान माध्यमों को भी प्रोत्साहन मिला। नोटबंदी ने आर्थिक गतिविधियों के औपचारीकरण और डिजिटल अवसंरचना के विस्तार के माध्यम से भारत की विशाल अनौपचारिक अर्थव्यवस्था को औपचारिक बैंकिंग प्रणाली से जोड़कर दीर्घकालिक पारदर्शिता को बढ़ावा दिया गया।
अवैध धन को वैध बनाने की गतिविधियों को रोकने के लिए कड़े सुरक्षा उपाय अपनाए गए। बड़ी धनराशियों को सीधे बैंक खातों में जमा कराया गया तथा बैंक काउंटर पर नोट बदलने के लिए पैन कार्ड या वैध पहचान-पत्र के माध्यम से आवश्यक विवरण प्रस्तुत करना अनिवार्य किया गया।
सरकार का मूल सिद्धांत नागरिक-केंद्रित शासन पर आधारित है।

5. ⁠सरकार ने बैंक लॉकरों की सुरक्षा के लिए सख्त व्यवस्था लागू की है। बैंक लॉकर सुरक्षित वॉल्ट/स्ट्रॉन्ग रूम में रखे जाते हैं, जहां CCTV, अलार्म सिस्टम, नियमित ऑडिट तथा हर लॉकर संचालन पर SMS/E-mail अलर्ट जैसी सुविधाएं उपलब्ध हैं। 
RBI मास्टर डायरेक्शन के अनुसार, मौजूदा ग्राहकों के लिए संशोधित लॉकर एग्रीमेंट निष्पादित करने में लगने वाले स्टाम्प पेपर का खर्च बैंकों द्वारा वहन किया जाता है।
लॉकर शुल्क नाममात्र के होते हैं और इनमें हर साल बदलाव नहीं किया जाता; आमतौर पर ये कई वर्षों तक एक जैसे ही बने रहते हैं।
बैकों के लॉकर में सामाग्री का नुकसान होना एक अपवादहै। यदि बैंक की सेवा में कमी के कारण लॉकर की सामग्री का नुकसान होता है, तो बैंक ग्राहकों को मुआवजा देने के लिए जिम्मेदार होते हैं। RBI के वर्तमान नियमों के अनुसार मुआवजा लॉकर के वार्षिक किराये के 100 गुना तक हो सकता है।

6. RBI ने पैसे की धोखाधड़ी और आतंकवाद फंडिंग को रोकने के लिए KYC दिशा-निर्देश बनाए हैं। इन दिशा-निर्देशों के अनुसार, KYC के लिए कई तरह के दस्तावेज़ इस्तेमाल किए जा सकते हैं। KYC को समय-समय पर अपडेट किया जाता है ताकि ग्राहकों की जानकारी या डेटा प्रासंगिक रहे। KYC को ब्रांच या बिना ब्रांच गए भी अपडेट किया जा सकता है। ग्राहकों की सुविधा के लिए, बैंकों ने वीडियो KYC और डिजिटल चैनलों के जरिए घर पर KYC जैसी कई सुविधाएँ शुरू की हैं। ज्यादातर खाते, जैसे जन धन खाते, में KYC केवल 8-10 साल में केवल एक बार अपडेट करना होता है।

वरिष्ठ नागरिक के अगर फिंगरप्रिंट या आइरिस में मिलान नहीं होता, तो बैंक ऑफलाइन वेरिफिकेशन करके या ग्राहक से किसी अन्य प्रमाणित दस्तावेज की कॉपी लेकर KYC अपडेट करते हैं।
ईज रिफॉर्म्स ने कस्टमर सर्विस, टेक्नोलॉजी और रिस्क मैनेजमेंट सुधारा है। नॉमिनेशन प्रक्रिया सरल कर 4 नॉमिनी जोड़ने का प्रावधान किया गया है, जिससे क्लेम सेटलमेंट आसान हुआ है। केवाईसी सरल और डिजिटल हो रही है।

7. ⁠सरकार बेहतर गवर्नेंस, ग्राहकों को अच्छी सेवा देने, तकनीकी आधुनिकीकरण और कामकाज की कार्यक्षमता में सुधार के जरिए बैंकों को मजबूत करने के लिए प्रतिबद्ध है। सरकार ने EASE (एनहैंस्ड एक्सेस एंड सर्विस एक्सीलेंस) एजेंडे और अन्य गवर्नेंस/ढांचागत पहलों के तहत सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों (PSBs) को मजबूत करने के लिए व्यापक सुधार किए हैं। इनका उद्देश्य इन बैंकों की कार्यक्षमता, जोखिम प्रबंधन के तरीकों और क्रेडिट अनुशासन में सुधार लाना है।

2014-15 में, भारतीय बैंकिंग क्षेत्र, विशेष रूप से सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंक (PSBs), फंसे हुए कर्ज के बढ़ते स्तर के कारण भारी दबाव में थे। सरकार ने अथक प्रयासों से इस समस्या से निपटने के लिए व्यापक कदम उठाए। इन पहलों की बदौलत, सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों ने वित्त वर्ष 2025-26 में 1.98 लाख करोड़ रुपये का अब तक का सबसे अधिक मुनाफा दर्ज किया। साथ ही, 31 मार्च 2026 तक उनका GNPA अनुपात 1.93% के स्तर पर आ गया, जो कई दशकों में सबसे निचला स्तर है। यह बदलाव साफ-सुथरी बैलेंस शीट और मजबूत क्रेडिट ग्रोथ की वजह से संभव हो पाया। सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों ने अपने वित्तीय और परिचालन प्रदर्शन में काफी सुधार किया है, जिससे वे मुनाफे में आ गए हैं और उनकी पूंजी की स्थिति भी मजबूत हुई है।

आरआरबी के पुनर्गठन से 'एक प्रदेश एक आरआरबी' का लक्ष्य साकार हुआ और आरआरबीज ने वित्तीय वर्ष 2025-26 में 10 हजार करोड़ से अधिक का सर्वाधिक लाभ दर्ज किया है।

सरकार बैंक कर्मचारियों के योगदान को मानती है। व्यापक पारदर्शी नियम लागू हैं ताकि किसी बैंककर्मी को गलत तरीके से दंडित न किया जा सके।

8. ⁠ग्राहक राष्ट्रीय हेल्पलाइन नंबर 1930 के जरिए, या बैंकों के अपने माध्यमों (जैसे कॉल सेंटर और शाखाओं) से डिजिटल वित्तीय धोखाधड़ी की रिपोर्ट कर सकते हैं। सुरक्षित डिजिटल बैंकिंग को बढ़ावा देने और धोखाधड़ी को रोकने के लिए, RBI और बैंक विज्ञापनों, SMS, WhatsApp, ईमेल और अन्य माध्यमों से ग्राहकों को जागरूक करने का काम करते हैं।
डिजिटल इंडिया के सिस्टम वैश्विक पहचान बना रहे हैं । यूपीआई ने तेज और सुरक्षित पेमेंट व्यवस्था तैयार की है। आज भारत में हर दिन लगभग 80 करोड़ से अधिक यूपीआई ट्रांजेक्शन हो रहे हैं । वैश्विक स्तर पर रियल-टाइम पेमेंट ट्रांजेक्शन वॉल्यूम में यूपीआई की हिस्सेदारी लगभग 49 प्रतिशत है, और इसका विस्तार 11 देशों में हो चुका है।
इस तरह की धोखाधड़ी को रोकने के लिए कई सुरक्षा उपाय किए गए हैं, जिनमें टू-फैक्टर ऑथेंटिकेशन, ट्रांजैक्शन अलर्ट और संदिग्ध गतिविधियों की पहचान करने वाले सिस्टम शामिल हैं। UPI ट्रांजैक्शन से जुड़ी धोखाधड़ी को रोकने के लिए, NPCI ने मोबाइल नंबर और डिवाइस के बीच 'डिवाइस बाइंडिंग', PIN के जरिए टू-फैक्टर ऑथेंटिकेशन, और दैनिक ट्रांजैक्शन लिमिट जैसी व्यवस्थाएं लागू की हैं। इसके अलावा, RBI के निर्देशों में अनधिकृत इलेक्ट्रॉनिक बैंकिंग ट्रांजैक्शन से बचाव के उपाय बताए गए हैं, जिनमें ग्राहकों की जिम्मेदारी और मुआवजे से जुड़े नियम शामिल हैं।
साइबर वित्तीय धोखाधड़ी से निपटने के लिए 'सिटिजन फाइनेंशियल साइबर फ्रॉड रिपोर्टिंग एंड मैनेजमेंट सिस्टम' (CFCFRMS) विकसित किया गया है और इसे लागू किया गया है। यह सिस्टम बैंकिंग नेटवर्क के जरिए धोखाधड़ी वाले ट्रांजैक्शन को तुरंत ब्लॉक करने में मदद करता है, जिससे पीड़ितों के पैसे सुरक्षित वापस मिलने की संभावना बढ़ जाती है। साथ ही, CFCFRMS के तहत बनाए गए 'मनी रिस्टोरेशन मॉड्यूल' (MRM) और 'ग्रीवेंस रिड्रेसल मॉड्यूल' (GRM) यह सुनिश्चित करते हैं कि शिकायतों का समय पर समाधान हो और पीड़ितों को उनके पैसे जल्द वापस मिल सकें।

9. ⁠क्रेडिट सुविधाएं देने के संबंध में दिशा-निर्देश संबंधित बैंकों की बोर्ड-अनुमोदित नीतियों के अनुसार होते हैं, जिनमें कोई भेदभाव नहीं किया जाता। इसके अलावा, भारतीय रिज़र्व बैंक (RBI) द्वारा पर्याप्त नियमन और निगरानी की व्यवस्था है। RBI की ओर से निर्धारित 'ड्यू डिलिजेंस' (जांच-पड़ताल) और 'क्रेडिट अप्रेजल' (ऋण मूल्यांकन) के नियम सभी ऋण आवेदकों पर समान रूप से लागू होते हैं।

हालांकि, बैंकों द्वारा छोटे ऋणों (small ticket loans) को आसानी से मंज़ूरी देने और उनकी प्रक्रिया को तेज़ करने के लिए कई कदम उठाए गए हैं, जिनमें 'ड्यू डिलिजेंस' की प्रक्रियाओं को कुछ हद तक सरल बनाना भी शामिल है।
सरकार ने किसानों, छोटे व्यवसायों, रेहड़ी-पटरी वालों, कारीगरों और उद्यमियों के लिए बिना किसी गिरवी (collateral-free) के ऋण उपलब्ध कराने के उद्देश्य से कई योजनाएं शुरू की हैं, जैसे- PM मुद्रा योजना, KCC, PM स्वनिधि, PM विश्वकर्मा और स्टैंड-अप इंडिया। प्रधान मंत्री मुद्रा योजना ने स्वरोजगार के लिए बिना कोलेटरल ऋण उपलब्ध करवाकर छोटे उद्यमियों को अपना कारोबार आगे बढ़ाने का अवसर दिया; 60 करोड़ से अधिक खातों में 43 लाख करोड़ रुपये से अधिक के ऋण स्वीकृत हुए हैं।  प्रधान मंत्री स्वनिधि योजना द्वारा पहली बार रेहड़ी पटरी वालों को आसान शर्तों पर सस्ता ऋण मिला है। 2030 तक बढ़ाई गई इस योजना में यूपीआई रुपे क्रेडिट कार्ड का प्रावधान है और स्विनिधि योजना के तहत 1 करोड़ से अधिक ऋण स्वीकृत हुए हैं। पीएम विश्वकर्मा योजना ने 18 पारंपरिक व्यवसायों के शिल्पकारों को आधुनिक औजार और नए बाजार से ताकत दी है; 6 लाख से ज्यादा लाभार्थियों को 5 हजार करोड़ से अधिक के ऋण स्वीकृत हुए हैं। समावेशी सुधारों के तहत एमएसएमई को बिना कागजी झंझट के त्वरित ऋण मिल रहा है, New Credit Assessment Model के अंतर्गत 9 लाख से अधिक खातों में 1 लाख 32 हजार करोड़ से अधिक ऋण स्वीकृत हुए हैं। माइक्रो एंटरप्राइज़ के लिए 5 लाख तक के क्रेडिट कार्ड की शुरुआत हुई है। सरकार की 'इमरजेंसी क्रेडिट लाइन गारंटी स्कीम' ने बाहरी व्यवधानों से प्रभावित व्यवसायों को लक्षित क्रेडिट गारंटी सहायता प्रदान की है।
सरकार ने सभी बड़े धोखेबाजों और ऋण चूककर्ताओं से निपटने के लिए कड़े कानून बनाए हैं एवं ऐसे सभी लोगों के खिलाफ सख्त कार्रवाई की जाती है।

10. ⁠बैंकों द्वारा बांटी जा रही बीमा पॉलिसियां पूरी तरह से ग्राहकों की सहमति से ही दी जाती हैं। भारतीय रिज़र्व बैंक (RBI) बैंकों द्वारा बीमा उत्पादों की बिक्री के लिए दिशा-निर्देश तय करता है। अगर गलत तरीके से बीमा बेचने (mis-selling) की कोई शिकायत आती है, तो उसे बैंकों की शिकायत निवारण प्रणाली और लागू नियामक ढांचे के जरिए सुलझाया जाता है।

आम आदमी की सामाजिक सुरक्षा को बढ़ाने के उद्देश्य से, 2015 में प्रधान मंत्री सुरक्षा बीमा योजना (PMSSBY)और प्रधानमंत्री जीवन ज्योति बीमा योजना (PMJJBY) शुरू की गईं। इनके जरिए कम लागत वाला और किफायती बीमा कवर उपलब्ध कराया गया है, जिसके तहत अब तक PMJJBY में 27 करोड़ से ज्यादा और PMSBY में 58 करोड़ से ज्यादा लोगों ने पंजीकरण कराया है। अटल पेंशन योजना से जुड़ने वालों की संख्या 9.5 करोड़ से अधिक हो चुकी है।

11. ⁠सरकार सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के कर्मचारियों का कल्याण सुनिश्चित करने के लिए प्रतिबद्ध है। सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों (PSBs) के कर्मचारियों को अच्छा वेतन मिलता है और समाज में उनका सम्मान है। सरकार सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के कर्मचारियों से जुड़े सभी HR मुद्दों को हल करने के लिए ठोस प्रयास करती रही है । इन बैंकों के कर्मचारियों की अधिकांश मांगें पूरी की गई हैं। पिछले 12 वर्षों में, सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों ने लगभग 5 लाख कर्मचारियों की भर्ती की है।

सरकार ने लोकतांत्रिक और भागीदारीपूर्ण तरीकों के माध्यम से सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों के कर्मचारियों के कल्याण के लिए लगातार कदम उठाए हैं, ताकि वेतन और उससे जुड़े लाभों में नियमित और समयबद्ध संशोधन सुनिश्चित किया जा सके। कर्मचारियों की भर्ती, पदोन्नति और स्थानांतरण में पारदर्शिता लाने के लिए व्यवस्थाओं को और मजबूत किया गया है।
⁠
12. बैंक ज़ीरो-बैलेंस बचत खाते (जैसे कि 'बेसिक सेविंग्स बैंक डिपॉजिट अकाउंट्स' या BSBDA और 'प्रधानमंत्री जन धन योजना' यानी PMJDY के तहत खोले गए खाते) उपलब्ध कराते हैं। इनका उद्देश्य यह सुनिश्चित करना है कि बैंकिंग सुविधाओं तक सबकी पहुँच हो—खासकर उन लोगों की, जिनकी अब तक बैंकिंग सेवाओं तक पहुँच नहीं थी, जो कमज़ोर वर्ग से आते हैं या जो छोटी बचत करने वाले हैं। साथ ही, इसका मकसद किफायती और आसानी से उपलब्ध बैंकिंग सेवाओं के ज़रिए वित्तीय समावेशन (financial inclusion) को बढ़ावा देना है। जन धन खातों पर कोई जुर्माना (पेनल्टी) नहीं लगता।

वित्तीय साक्षरता, वित्तीय समावेशन, सुरक्षित डिजिटल बैंकिंग और ग्राहकों की सुविधा को बढ़ावा देने के लिए, बैंक नियमित रूप से ग्राहकों को जागरूक करने के अभियान चलाते हैं। इसमें ग्राम पंचायत स्तर पर कैंप, मास मीडिया अभियान, SMS और ईमेल शामिल हैं। इसके अलावा, 'वित्तीय साक्षरता केंद्र' (FLCs) अलग-अलग समूहों के लिए विशेष कैंप लगाते हैं, जहाँ क्षेत्रीय भाषाओं में जानकारी दी जाती है। साथ ही, RBI के 'इलेक्ट्रॉनिक बैंकिंग अवेयरनेस एंड ट्रेनिंग' (e-BAAT) कार्यक्रम भी चलाए जाते हैं। किसान क्रेडिट कार्ड और कृषि ऋण से छोटे किसानों को सस्ता ऋण मिला, जिसमें डेयरी, मुर्गी व मत्स्यपालन भी शामिल हैं। वित्त वर्ष 25-26 में कृषि ऋण वितरण 30 लाख करोड़ रुपये तक पहुँचा और 7 करोड़ 28 लाख से अधिक केसीसी खाते सक्रिय हैं। स्टैंड-अप इंडिया के तहत अनुसूचित वर्ग के लोगों और महिला उद्यमियों के लिए 2.7 लाख से अधिक ऋण स्वीकृत हुए, जिनमें 82 प्रतिशत ऋण महिला उद्यमियों को मिले है।

ये 12 स्पष्टीकरण एक ऐसी बैंकिंग प्रणाली को दर्शाते हैं जो अधिक मजबूत है, जिसकी पहुंच आसान है और जो जनता की जरूरतों के प्रति लगातार अधिक संवेदनशील होती जा रही है।
सरकार के लगातार हस्तक्षेप और बैंकिंग सुधारों की मदद से मार्च 2026 में PSBs का जीएनपीए (GNPA) न्यूनतम स्तर 1.93% पहुंच गया है। साथ ही, वित्त वर्ष 2025-26 में इन बैंकों ने ₹1.98 लाख करोड़ का अब तक का सबसे net profit कमाया है और इनका कुल Business ₹283 लाख करोड़ तक पहुंच गया है। इसके साथ ही, वित्तीय समावेशन (financial inclusion) की उपलब्धियों से आम नागरिकों को भी काफी फायदा हुआ है। इसमें 59 करोड़ से अधिक जन धन खाते, 59 करोड़ से अधिक मुद्रा लोन और अकेले वित्त वर्ष 2025-26 में 24,000 करोड़ से अधिक UPI ट्रांजेक्शन शामिल हैं। इन सभी प्रयासों के चलते, वित्तीय समावेशन सूचकांक (Financial Inclusion Index) में भारी उछाल आया है, जो 2017 में 43.4 था और 2026 में बढ़कर 70.0 हो गया है।

7. ⁠जानबूझकर बैंक को बीमार क्यों किया गया है? स्टाफ़ पर कामचोरी का आरोप लगाकर ईमानदार और सत्यनिष्ठ बैंक कर्मचारियों को योजना बनाकर क्यों बदनाम किया गया? सर्वर डाउन है, प्रिंटर ख़राब है, ओटीपी नहीं आ रहा, आज काम बहुत है कल आइएगा जैसी समस्याओं के नाम पर सालों से विश्वसनीय बैंकों को कमज़ोर क्यों किया गया और कमीशन लेकर बैंक बेचने का जुगाड़ क्यों किया गया?

AN APOLOGY IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR CONSTITUTIONAL COMPLIANCE: SUPREME COURT EXPOSES EXECUTIVE OVERREACH IN DELHI INTERNET BAN

The unfolding of this episode is a telling commentary on the precarious state of our constitutional governance. That the government, faced with the judicial scrutiny of an internet ban—a measure that strikes at the very root of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a)—has chosen to tender an unconditional apology, is a tacit admission of executive overreach.
 
However, an apology, however unconditional, cannot act as a panacea for a constitutional transgression. It is deeply concerning that an order imposing a blanket internet shutdown in the capital—crippling the flow of information and stifling dissent—was passed, seemingly without the application of mind, only to be withdrawn or apologized for once the judicial microscope was applied.
 
The Supreme Court is not merely a forum for dispute resolution; it is the ultimate sentinel on the qui vive, the guardian of the citizen's liberties against the might of the State. While the unconditional apology is noted, the Court must not allow this hasty retreat to bury the larger, grave questions of proportionality and legality under the guise of commotion.

The issuance of notice in the connected matters is a welcome step. The majesty of the Constitution demands that the executive be held accountable, for the rule of law cannot be reduced to a mere game of catch-me-if-you-can, where the State breaches fundamental rights and then seeks to absolve itself through a written apology.

#CJPProtests #DelhiInternetBan #InternetShutdown #CentralDelhi #NarendraKumarGoswami #UnconditionalApology #SupremeCourtHearing #GovernmentAffidavit #Item22 #Item23

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

But he defends the shutdown as proportionate and seeks modification of the October 11 order to permit internet suspension "in situations of necessity"

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

An “unconditional apology” — but the government still wants the right to shut down the internet again. What exactly is the Supreme Court being asked to accept?
In a marathon hearing before CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, the Supreme Court questioned the Centre’s apology in the contempt case over the internet shutdown. Justice Bagchi pointed out that defending the government’s actions made the apology appear qualified rather than unconditional.
But that was only the beginning.
🔹 Rahul Gandhi’s SIR petition: The Supreme Court issued notice on a provisional basis, subject to a petitioner explaining his conduct at the next hearing.
🔹 Jantar Mantar protests: The government said the decision to de-notify the protest site was based on a committee report prepared before the court’s observations. The court issued notice but did not order its restoration.
🔹 CCTV footage: All law enforcement agencies were directed to preserve CCTV footage and other digital material related to the events.
🔹 Section 172 of the BNSS: The Supreme Court agreed to examine the constitutional challenge to the provision, observing that it must be read in light of the Constitution.
🔹 Section 163 and the detentions: During the hearing, the Solicitor General said the relevant notification was not on record, even as questions were raised over the detention of nearly 3,000 people.
Meanwhile, petitions concerning AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and the Election Commission were separated for consideration on another date.
The court took up several crucial issues, but major questions remain unanswered. Why seek permission for future internet shutdowns while offering an unconditional apology? And should Rahul Gandhi’s petition against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar remain provisional until he explains his conduct?
Is this accountability—or another delay in addressing the central questions? Share your views in the comments.

STORY | Timely, lawful measures averted major public order situation in capital: Delhi Police to SC

Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar has told the Supreme Court that timely, proportionate and lawful measures taken by the police helped avert a major public order situation during the recent protests in the national capital.

The commissioner, who tendered an unconditional and unqualified apology to the apex court in a contempt case, said that preventive measures undertaken on October 10, when the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) gave a protest call, were based on intelligence inputs and an assessment of the prevailing and ever-changing ground situation.

In an affidavit filed in the top court, Kumar referred to the steps taken by the police administration, including regulation of Metro rail services in Delhi.

“These measures were directed towards maintaining peace and tranquillity and preventing any disturbance of public order in the national capital,” he said.

The efforts made, and the actions taken by the police, deserve to be viewed in the context of the fact that Delhi is the capital of the country and that every national capital carries its own sensitivities, the commissioner said.

“No police administration can permit any breach of public order in the national capital, particularly when a call is given by an organisation with a recent history of mob violence, destruction of public and private property, and incidents resulting in injuries to several individuals and the subsequent events of October 6, 7 and 8,” the affidavit said.

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Check shared bundle components: one stockout could take several offers offline.

Align VIP early access, the main promotion, and existing customer demand in one allocation plan shared by marketing, purchasing, and fulfillment.

Anjali Bhardwaj & Amrita Johri have moved the Supreme Court against requiring voters excluded in SIR to use Form 6, arguing it forces them to falsely declare they are first time applicants. Prashant Bhushan will mention the matter tomorrow. 

The petition states that 47,56,722 voters, 32.78% of Delhi’s pre-SIR electorate were excluded from the draft roll under the Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate (ASDD) category. To seek restoration, they must submit Form 6, which requires them to declare that they are applying for inclusion for the first time.
The petition argues that this forces previously registered voters to make a factually incorrect declaration, potentially exposing them to penalties for false declarations under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. It also challenges the additional declaration required with Forms 6 and 8 during SIR, arguing that it was introduced without following the legally mandated rule making procedure. It questions why different requirements apply during SIR and non-SIR periods.

The ongoing voter verification exercise raises an important question.
Every birth and death in India is required to be reported to Municipal Authorities, Gram Panchayats, and the Registrar of Births & Deaths. Death records are already maintained in government databases. In many cases, families have seen names removed from records after a death is registered.
If government departments already possess this information, why can't the Election Commission periodically cross-check electoral rolls with official death records and automatically remove deceased voters?
Similarly, if citizenship and identity records are available through various government databases, technology can be used to identify duplicate, fraudulent, or ineligible entries in a transparent manner.
Instead, asking ordinary citizens to repeatedly prove their eligibility creates inconvenience and may leave room for errors, omissions, or allegations of political manipulation.
A modern digital democracy should strive for: ✅ Automatic updating of voter rolls from authenticated government records ✅ Removal of deceased voters through official death registrations ✅ Transparency in electoral roll management ✅ Minimum burden on genuine citizens ✅ Equal treatment of all voters
Clean electoral rolls are essential, but the responsibility should primarily rest with institutions that already hold the relevant data, rather than placing the burden on citizens.
Let us encourage efficient governance, transparency, and protection of every eligible citizen's voting rights.
Forward if you agree that technology should make voter list management more accurate and citizen-friendly.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

5. INDIAS PROBABLE SECURITY CONCERNS OVER STARLINK 

Whilst I am not privy to the security concerns of the Union Home Ministry and the CCCS (does it even exist anymore ?), some of the probable concerns are listed below.

a. The concern of whether India can maintain control over national security, communications, data, and spectrum while allowing a foreign-operated satellite network to provide internet across the country is a major worry.

b. National Security and Military Use 
-India will need to identify and investigate the misuse of satellite terminals.
-They will have to respond to lawful government orders to restrict service in specific locations or to specific users.
- They will have to prevent unauthorized communications from undermining military operations.
-Ensure that terminals and services are not being used to facilitate terrorism, smuggling, or other serious crimes.

This is not a hypothetical fear, as @Jairam_Ramesh   had correctly pointed out that Starlink equipment was recovered from Manipur in 2024, and also more recently  during a drug-related operation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. 

c. Data Sovereignity and Protection 

The former MP @priyankac19 had raised some important questions in the Parliament on this aspect. 

India has to ensure that communications generated by Indian users remain subject to Indian law and that authorised agencies can obtain access when legally required.

The govt had replied on 7/8/2025 to Ms.Chaturvedi,  specifying security conditions for Starlink, including:
-Indian user traffic must not be routed through gateways outside India.
-Indian data must not be copied and decrypted outside India.
-Indian user traffic must not be mirrored to systems or servers abroad

https://t.co/2q54VIBAH3

d. Can India switch Starlink off during a crisis?
This is a major concern for India, because as we have seen, during times of local crisis or military insurgency, the Govt has switched off Internet!

Retaining operational control during a war, border confrontation, terrorist incident, or other emergency is critical.

e. Foreign ownership and strategic dependence

Starlink is operated by SpaceX, a US company owned & controlled by Elon Musk. This brings into question the  foreign ownership, corporate accountability, and dependence on infrastructure outside India's direct control.

In a Musk company, the govt has no clarity on who ultimately controls the service and its technical operations. Do ownership and investment structures meet India's foreign investment rules?

It's also important whether sensitive operational information could be accessed by foreign entities or enemy entities, and what remedies would India have if the operator failed to comply with its license conditions?

f. The risk of a foreign company becoming strategically indispensable

Starlink's network is via a global constellation and centralized service-management systems. India's reliance on one foreign provider could create strategic vulnerabilities if access were disrupted, commercial terms changed, or international relations deteriorated.

The issue of pricing and accessibility is also a concern but less pressing than the security concerns.

People forget that the Use of SAT PHONES is still banned in India, and SatComs use Iridium and Inmarsat satellite networks.

Starlink is the next level beyond that and will facilitate internet and communication through LEO (low Earth orbits).

Personally, I believe that India must ensure at least a 30% domestic shareholding in any such company and a local earth station in India to route all data through. If Namibia and South Africa can demand these terms, then surely India must.

In the end, @elonmusk & @SpaceX @SpaceXStarlink will have to comply with the demands of the Indian Government, just as @reliancejio & @airtelindia have to.

The brouhaha & insults over the last 3 days have been a total waste of time and a highly counterproductive exercise for Elon, SpaceX, and Starlink. 

They should've learned from the Trump & trade deal examples; it just rubbed people the wrong way and also polarized a lot of opinion against Musk and Starlink. 

Sometimes it needs more than money, genius and power to deal with India, it needs common sense. !

JAI HIND ! 

4/4 end of thread

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

THE AI SCHOOL PROJECT 📚

My son asked an AI to help with his history assignment. What it uncovered made my father lock himself in his bedroom—and beg us to delete the evidence.

Son: “It says Grandpa was there.”

Me: “Where?”

Son: “At the protest.”

Me: “Grandpa never told us that.”

Son: “The AI found his name in footage.”

Me: “Show me.”

He turned his laptop toward me.

The screen showed a grainy black-and-white photograph of a crowded street. People were running. Police officers stood behind a line of shields.

Then my eyes landed on a young man holding a cardboard sign.

It was my father.

I recognized his face immediately, even though the photograph was decades old.

Me: “Where did you find this?”

Son: “The AI matched his face with an old newspaper archive.”

I zoomed in.

My father was holding a sign that read: WE KNOW WHO STOLE THE MONEY.

“Which protest was this?” I asked.

My son read the information displayed beneath the image.

“Thirty years ago. Students and workers protested after a public fund disappeared.”

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post
